title: One tree, every path
subtitle: Learn the filesystem hierarchy, move with intent, and know which directories matter.
objectives: Use absolute and relative paths correctly
Navigate with pwd, cd, and directory shortcuts
Identify the purpose of the major RHEL directories

commands.desc: Print the physical working directory path.
Change to an absolute directory path.
List all files, long format, human-readable sizes.
Show filesystem type, size, and usage.
Show block devices, filesystems, UUIDs, and mounts.

lab.title: Map an unfamiliar system
lab.scenario: You have landed on a host you did not build. Build a mental map before changing anything.

steps.text: Start at the root and list the top-level directories.
steps.verify: You should see etc, var, home, usr, boot, and the virtual directories.

steps.text: Identify the filesystem backing / and its usage.
steps.verify: The device and filesystem type should match between the two commands.

steps.text: Inspect /var/log as a directory entry, then list its contents.
steps.verify: The first command describes the directory; the second describes its files.

steps.text: Find the ten largest entries directly under /var.
steps.verify: du can take time on a busy host; note which directory is largest.

steps.text: Return to your home directory and confirm where you are.
steps.verify: pwd should print /home/<user>, and cd ~ should return there from any directory.

quiz.q: What is the difference between /var/log and /var/log/messages?
options: One is a directory, one is a file
quiz.why: /var/log is a directory containing log files; /var/log/messages is a file within it on traditional RHEL configurations.

quiz.q: Which command reports filesystem capacity and type?
quiz.why: df reports filesystem-level capacity. du reports directory consumption; free reports memory.

options: It returns to the previous working directory
quiz.why: The shell remembers the previous directory; cd - switches back to it.
